analysis.one_liner: Requires judges to sanction attorneys who file unsupported federal claims and pay the other side's costs.
analysis.headline: The bill went no further than its first day: referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on February 5, 2015, it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite Rule 11 of the federal court rules so that judges must — not may — sanction any attorney, law firm, or party who files a claim or representation the court finds unsupported, and any sanction would have to compensate the other side, including reasonable attorneys' fees. It would also delete the 'safe harbor' that currently lets a lawyer withdraw or fix a challenged paper within 21 days and avoid sanctions. Sponsors framed it as deterring meritless lawsuits; the mandatory fee-shifting and the loss of the safe harbor also raise the cost and risk of bringing hard-to-prove cases against well-resourced defendants.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses and other defendants facing federal lawsuits, and their insurers: every suit filed against them would carry a new, mandatory risk that the plaintiff's side pays their legal fees if a judge finds part of the case unsupported.

how_it_helps.text: Makes Rule 11 sanctions mandatory ('shall' instead of 'may') and requires any sanction to compensate parties injured by the violation, including reasonable attorneys' fees and costs.
Removes the 21-day safe harbor that currently allows a lawyer to withdraw or correct a challenged filing and avoid sanctions, so the sanction threat applies from the moment a paper is filed.
Authorizes additional sanctions — striking pleadings, dismissing the suit, nonmonetary directives, or penalty payments to the court — when warranted for deterrence.
The bill's own text states it does not bar or impede the development of new claims, defenses, or remedies, including civil rights claims.

analysis.who_pays: Plaintiffs and their attorneys, who would face mandatory fee payments for any representation a judge finds unsupported, with no chance to correct it first. People bringing civil rights, employment, or injury claims against large defendants would bear the most risk, since those cases are often difficult to prove at the outset.

drawbacks.text: Without the 21-day safe harbor, the fee-shifting penalty attaches before a lawyer can withdraw or fix a challenged claim, which legal commentators across the spectrum warned would deter attorneys from taking legitimate but factually difficult cases — the cases ordinary people most need, such as civil rights and employment claims against large institutions.

The rule-of-construction section of the bill itself acknowledges the risk, expressly stating that nothing in it should be construed to bar or impede the assertion of new claims, defenses, or remedies under federal, state, or local law, including civil rights laws.

Federal judges already have discretion to sanction truly abusive filings; converting 'may' to 'shall' removes that judgment, so a judge who thinks a borderline claim was filed in good faith would still be required to penalize the lawyer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem — filings made without a factual or legal basis — and compensating victims of such filings has intuitive appeal. But the design cuts broadly: mandatory sanctions plus the loss of the safe harbor transfer fee risk onto plaintiffs' counsel in any case where a judge finds a piece of a complaint unsupported, and the hardest cases to prove at the outset are typically those brought by individuals against institutions. The deterrence gain and the access-to-courts cost pull strongly in opposite directions, and the bill never faced a hearing or vote where that trade-off could be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the same day, and the committee — chaired by the bill's own lead sponsor — never took it up before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Grassley introduced the bill in the Senate on February 5, 2015, joined by Sen. Marco Rubio.
It was its first and only action: the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary that day.
No further actions — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appear in the record through the end of the 114th Congress.
The bill had one cosponsor in total.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defendants facing federal lawsuits — and the insurers who cover them — because the existing Rule 11 rules, including the safe harbor that lets lawyers correct filings before penalty, stayed in place. Plaintiffs and their attorneys also kept the current, more forgiving sanction regime.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-IA), lead sponsor and Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and shepherded it into the Judiciary Committee he chaired; the record shows no further action on it under his chairmanship.

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only additional supporter.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing or markup — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters were Republicans — Grassley as sponsor and Rubio as the lone cosponsor — and no Democrat signed on, though the bill also never drew any recorded opposition.

industries.note: Mandatory fee-shifting and the end of the safe harbor would raise the price of suing large companies, insurance carriers, and institutions, shrinking the number of claims filed against them. Their benefit comes at the cost of individuals' access to federal court.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' law firms and the civil litigation bar
industries.note: These firms take cases — often civil rights, employment, and injury claims — on contingency and absorb the risk that a claim may not hold up; mandatory sanctions payable to the defense would make many of those cases financially impossible to bring.
The bill's rule-of-construction section protects the development of civil rights claims on paper, but the practical fee risk on their attorneys would likely reduce the number brought.
